lines.text: cheerful gathering of the family circle or the meeting of
friends, or the gifts of noble art—all that we may enjoy on
the Lord's Day also, if we enjoy it as the Lord's gift for which
we thank Him. "For all that the Lord created is good and
nothing is bad which s received with a grateful heart."
Only the pleasure in the enjoyment of which we could not
thank the Lord as Giver, nor indeed think of Him at all,
but would rather have to avoid all religious thoughts, is
"worldly pleasure" which we ought to shun not only on
Sunday but on weekdays also. And even other pleasures
which we might thankfully welcome as His gift become
"worldly pleasures", if in enjoying them we forget Him and
the thanks due to Him. "Whether then you eat or drink, or
whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." It is this
which we are to learn from the Lord; this is the meaning of
His yoke, and this should stand as the guiding and testing
rule over all that we do on the Lord's Day.
IV
And finally, one last word! Sunday should mean for us a
new beginning not merely in regard to our week-day work.
It is not simply the humdrum work of the week which
causes us to feel the blessing of a new beginning Sunday by
Sunday.
"A new beginning"-how often is that the wish of our
hearts when we look back on our past with all its working
days and Sundays! For how often do we realize with a
painful sense of oppression that we are caught in and
enchained by our past, that we have lost our way in life and
can find no means of escape from our difficulties. We have
enslaved ourselves to one thing or another-obligations,
customs, passions! We note that as a result we have become
fettered and dishonoured, that we are perishing, and cannot
get free from the toils. At such moments we are aware how
weary and heavy laden we in fact are, not only through work
and care but also-and still more oppressively-through
guilt and impurity. Oh that we might begin all over again!
